quote: 8.1 By Commerce One. Commerce One shall indemnify, defend and hold harmless Corio and its Customers from any and all damages, liabilities, costs and expenses (including reasonable attorneys' fees) incurred by Corio or its Customers arising out of any claim that the Software infringes any patent, copyright, trademark or trade right secret of a third party
rationale: Section 8.1 gives us (Corio) and our Customers a full defend-and-indemnify from Commerce One for third-party claims that the Software infringes patent, copyright, trademark or trade secret rights, with standard procedure (prompt notice, tender of control, cooperation at Vendor's expense, right to join with own counsel) and the usual remedy ladder (procure rights, replace/modify, or terminate with pro-rated refund of fees paid). The Section 8.2 carve-outs are customary (use outside the Documentation; modification by a third party) and are no broader than the exclusions the fallback tolerates. There is no reciprocal Corio indemnity for the Vendor's software, so the walk-away scenario (one-way Customer indemnity) does not arise. Section 9 expressly excludes "LIABILITY ARISING UNDER SECTION 8" from both the 12-month fee cap and the consequential-damages waiver, so the Vendor indemnity is uncapped — better than the fallback's 3x super-cap. The clause therefore satisfies the fallback and substantially reaches the preferred position on IP. Noted but not flagged: the indemnity does not extend to Vendor's breach of applicable law, unauthorised access to Corio data, or gross negligence/wilful misconduct, which are preferred-position add-ons rather than material failures of the fallback.

quote: 14.1 Assignment. Neither party may assign this Agreement or any rights or obligations hereunder, whether by operation of law or otherwise, without the prior written consent of the other party. Notwithstanding the foregoing, either party shall have the right to assign this Agreement in connection with the merger or acquisition of such party or the sale of all or substantially all of its assets related to this Agreement without such consent, except in the case where such transaction involves a direct competitor of the other party where consent of the other party will be required.
rationale: Section 14.1 is a mutual assignment clause that expressly permits either party — including us (Corio) — to assign the Agreement without consent in connection with a merger, acquisition or sale of all or substantially all assets related to the Agreement, so the M&A/successor carve-out the playbook requires is present and the walk-away case (blanket prohibition with no M&A carve-out) does not arise. Sections 11.2 and 11.3, and the Agreement generally, contain no change-of-control termination or re-pricing right for Commerce One (no "change of control" or "deemed an assignment" language anywhere in the document), so the second key risk is also absent. The clause therefore sits at the fallback (mutual successor assignment right, no notice condition even required) and largely at the preferred position. Two sub-preferred points, noted rather than flagged: there is no express carve-out allowing assignment to an affiliate without consent, and consent for other assignments is not qualified by a "not to be unreasonably withheld" standard; the direct-competitor consent requirement is reciprocal and mirrors the protection the playbook itself seeks against vendor assignments. These are minor gaps against preferred wording and do not defeat the fallback, so no redline is proposed.

rationale: The Agreement contains no liquidated damages, penalty, early-termination fee or minimum/shortfall payment obligation on our side. Fees payable by Corio (Sections 4.1–4.2 and Exhibit B/Payment Terms) are ordinary license, maintenance and revenue-share amounts, and Section 11 permits termination on breach or non-renewal with no termination charge or accelerated fee; Section 11.3 only continues fees for continuing use/support that we elect to receive. There is likewise no late-payment interest or penalty provision. The audit true-up in Section 4.2 (payment of a shortfall plus audit costs on a >5% underpayment) is a cost-recovery mechanic, not a liquidated damages or penalty amount. This meets the preferred position of no liquidated damages or penalties payable by the Customer, so no redline is proposed.

quote: 14.3 Choice of Law; Arbitration; Venue. This Agreement shall be governed by the laws of the State of California, USA, excluding conflict of laws provisions and excluding the 1980 United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods. Any disputes arising out of this Agreement shall be resolved by binding arbitration in accordance with the then-current commercial arbitration rules of the American Arbitration Association ("RULES"). The arbitration shall be conducted by one (1) arbitrator appointed in accordance with the Rules in San Francisco County, California.
rationale: Section 14.3 selects California law, which is expressly within the accepted list, and seats dispute resolution in San Francisco County, California — a domestic US forum with award enforcement available in the California courts. This sits at the playbook fallback (California law and forum) rather than the preferred position (New York law with exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts in New York County), so it is acceptable and not redlined. Two sub-elements fall short of the preferred wording but are not material failures: disputes go to mandatory single-arbitrator AAA arbitration rather than directly to court, and the venue for enforcement is San Francisco rather than New York County. Neither triggers the walk-away test, which is limited to a vendor home jurisdiction outside the accepted list with exclusive foreign venue or arbitration seated abroad; the seat here is domestic and California is not an off-list jurisdiction. Section 12 (source code escrow) refers disputes back to Section 14.3, so the same accepted forum governs throughout, and no competing jurisdiction clause appears elsewhere in the Agreement.

quote: Corio to pay Commerce One [*] of all Application Management Revenue from Corio Customers for use of Commerce One Software or MarketSite.net Service Access subject to the following limitations.
rationale: The Agreement imposes no minimum purchase commitment, take-or-pay obligation, or volume cap on us (Corio, the licensee). Our recurring payment to Commerce One is a pure revenue share — a percentage of Application Management Revenue actually received from Corio Customers (p0157), accruing only once a Corio Customer "begins live operations" (p0160) — with no floor, guarantee, or shortfall charge. Implementation fees are time-and-materials against an agreed Statement of Work with a not-to-exceed cap (p0161), i.e., ordered services only. Annual maintenance and support is expressly conditional on our election to keep paying ("provided that Corio continues to pay the annual Maintenance and Support fees," p0055), so we can exit that spend without penalty rather than being locked into five years of fees. Exhibit D's sales and marketing items, including the two-customer target, are stated to be "non-binding" and commercially-reasonable-efforts only (p0198, p0205). This satisfies the preferred position: fees are for usage or ordered services only. Two minor points noted but not flagged: (i) the sole "minimum" reference (p0158) is a metering convention — a 40 Authorized Software User floor per Customer applied when drawing down the initial 3000 licenses granted to us — which affects how quickly that royalty-free pool is consumed rather than obliging us to buy anything; and (ii) the only "shortfall" language is the reciprocal audit adjustment in §4.4 (p0059), which is a true-up ("the appropriate party shall promptly pay the amount of such shortfall or refund such overpayment") and not a penalty. No redline required.

Upon expiration or termination of this Agreement for any reason, and without limiting Corio's rights that survive under Section 11.3, Commerce One shall (i) at Corio's request, provide reasonable transition assistance to Corio and its Customers for a period of up to six (6) months at Commerce One's then-current standard rates; (ii) within thirty (30) days of Corio's written request, return to Corio all data of Corio, its Customers and Software Users in Commerce One's possession or control, together with Corio's Confidential Information, in a commonly used, machine-readable format; and (iii) thereafter delete such data and Confidential Information from its systems and certify such deletion to Corio in writing.

quote: Upon termination or expiration of this Agreement, each party shall otherwise return or destroy any Confidential Information of the other party provided, however, Corio may retain any Confidential Information necessary for Corio to continue supporting it's then-existing Customers.
rationale: The Agreement has no exit/transition clause. rationale: The Agreement contains no insurance clause: the outline shows no insurance heading, the only textual hit for "insurance" is an unrelated revenue deduction in the definitions (p0012), and neither Miscellaneous (Section 14) nor Shared Resources (Section 13) imposes any coverage obligation. Commerce One is the vendor here (Corio is the licensee/hosting customer): it supplies the Software and MarketSite service and provides operations, consulting and engineering personnel who work alongside Corio personnel and touch Corio's hosted environment and data, so this is squarely a services/hosting vendor for which the playbook expects coverage. Absence of any insurance for a vendor with access to our data is walk-away territory, so we inserted a short covenant at the preferred levels (CGL 1M/2M, E&O 2M, cyber 5M, workers' compensation, certificates on request) in Section 14, noting the E&O 1M / cyber 2M fallback is available. Numbering of the new clause can be conformed on execution.

rationale: The Section 2 grants run to Corio alone. Revocability is not a problem: Section 2.1 is expressly "perpetual and irrevocable" and Section 2.2 is "fully paid up, perpetual", and transferability meets the fallback because Section 14.1 permits assignment without consent on a merger, acquisition or sale of substantially all related assets (subject only to a direct-competitor consent carve-out). However, no provision extends the licence to our affiliates, there is no defined "Affiliate" and no written-notice mechanism to add them; Section 2.2 is confined to "Corio's internal business operations". Contractor use is addressed only indirectly (Corio Servers may be "owned or operated by or for Corio"). Affiliate coverage is a material term of both the preferred and fallback positions, so the grant fails the fallback on that element. Our minimal edit adds affiliates and contractors acting on our behalf to the internal use licence and leaves the rest of the grant structure, including the unlimited Customer sublicence, untouched.

rationale: Section 9 caps both parties, but the basis is not 12 months' fees: it is limited to amounts "ACTUALLY PAID BY CORIO ... FOR THE TRANSACTION WHICH THE LIABILITY RELATES TO", a per-transaction slice of fees that can fall well below even six months' fees and so fails the fallback on cap size (and risks walk-away territory for Commerce One's exposure). Carve-outs are also short of the fallback: only Section 8 (Commerce One's IP indemnity) sits outside the cap, while breach of the confidentiality obligation in Section 10, gross negligence, wilful misconduct and fraud are all capped. The mutual exclusion of indirect/consequential damages is acceptable. Our redline moves the cap to the preferred basis (greater of 12 months' fees paid or payable and USD 1,000,000) and adds Section 10, gross negligence, wilful misconduct and fraud as uncapped carve-outs, keeping the existing sentence structure. We did not add the "payment obligations are not damages" clarification, which is a minor sub-element rather than a separate deviation.

quote: 11.1 Term. The term of this Agreement shall commence on the Effective Date and shall continue in full force and effect for an initial period of five (5) years. Thereafter, this Agreement shall automatically renew for subsequent one (1) year periods unless either party provides the other party with written notification at least thirty (30) days prior to the expiration of the initial five (5) year term or any one (1) year renewal thereof of its intention to terminate this Agreement.
rationale: Section 11 gives Corio (our party, the licensee) no right to terminate for convenience during the five-year initial term: the only exits are non-renewal at the end of a term, material breach after a 30-day cure period, and insolvency. Absence of any customer convenience right in a multi-year term is walk-away territory under this rule, so it fails both the preferred (30 days' notice with pro-rata refund) and fallback (60–90 days' notice) positions. Commerce One likewise has no convenience right, which is consistent with the playbook and left unchanged. Redline inserts a new Section 11.4 giving Corio a 30-day convenience termination with refund of prepaid fees and confirming Commerce One has no mid-term convenience right; 60 days' notice is an acceptable fallback.

The locked preferred level is fully satisfied; no redline of the existing Sections 11.1–11.3 was needed and none was made, so untouched commercial terms (renewal, breach/insolvency termination, survival) remain effective. Minimality is slightly exceeded: the agreement already uses "Corio" for our party and separately defines "Customer" as Corio's customers, so the added definitional sentence redefining "Customer" for this Section is unnecessary boilerplate — simply naming "Corio" would suffice and would avoid overloading a defined term. Because the redefinition is expressly scoped "For purposes of this Section 11.4", it does not create an operative contradiction or dangling mechanic elsewhere, so intent is preserved.
